rail_guard.text: Aberdeen Station. It's the far end of the east coast line from London, and the platform is exactly as exposed as you'd expect.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited in Great Britain. Where to?

sailor.text: Orkney, is it? The Hjaltland Gull sails six hours north, and the gannets are free entertainment. Bring a jumper. Bring two.

then.text: See that? The granite's sparkling. Rain's the only polish this city needs, and we get it free.
Sun's out and the whole city's glittering like a sugar bowl. Shield your eyes, it's only granite.
Granite holds the day's warmth a wee while after dark. Lean on a wall, it's like a cosy grey hug.

granite_mason.text: {greeting} Aberdeen granite is grey, and hard as an argument. They built half of London's bridges from it, and the Terrace at the Houses of Parliament, and all our own grand buildings.
It sparkles when it's wet. Which, in Aberdeen, is Tuesday to Monday. We're not complaining. It sparkles more.

then.text: Fit like? Ye'll nae see much the day, the haar's in. Fit's that? Exactly, I cannae see it either.
Fit like? Hold on tae yer hat, loon. That wind's awa' tae Peterhead and it wants company.
Fit like this early? I'm up wi' the gulls. They're louder than me, but nae as polite.

doric_speaker.text: 'Fit like?' That's how we say 'how are you?' in Doric, the Aberdeen dialect. You answer, 'Nae bad, fit like yersel?', which is 'not bad, how are you?'.
A 'quine' is a girl and a 'loon' is a boy. 'Fit' means 'what', 'far' means 'where' and 'foo' means 'how'. It's not hard, just very fast.

then.text: Haar's in, so the foghorn's on. Mind your step on the quay, the edge is wetter than it looks.
North Sea's in a right temper the day. The supply boats are staying put, and so is my tea.
Lights coming on along the harbour now. Best time of day, if you ask me, and nobody does.

harbour_master.text: {greeting} It's the oldest business in Scotland, this harbour. We've shipped granite, herring, whisky and the occasional pony. Nowadays, it's supply boats and cruise ships.
Haar is what we call the sea fog that rolls in from the North Sea. A cold, wet blanket you can't see through. We love it, a bit. It's moody.

then.text: Glad I'm onshore this week. A gale on the rigs is like living inside a washing machine. A tall one.
Sunshine in Aberdeen! I'll tell the seagulls offshore. They won't believe me either.

oil_engineer.text: Aberdeen's the oil capital of Europe. Oil was found under the North Sea in 1969, and the city's been busy ever since. I work on the rigs two weeks on, two weeks off.
Two weeks offshore, and you start talking to the seagulls. They're surprisingly good listeners. I recommend them over most of my colleagues.

then.text: The Professor rang the post office, the harbour, and a pub. I'd say she's quite keen.
The south road's that way. Newcastle's a fortnight on foot, they tell me, but the Ministry of Plot Convenience has had a word, so it's more of a long afternoon.

else.text: A man in a postie's jacket is leaning against a bollard, holding a mobile phone out at arm's length as though it were a small, vocal animal.
Are you {player}? Ach, thank goodness. A woman in Macclesfield's rung every phone box in Aberdeen looking for you. She's beside herself. She says your phone's been off since Braemar.
Your phone buzzes at last. Professor Garside, who sounds as if she has run up a flight of stairs.
{player}! You're in Aberdeen! The Frost Stone, the Highlands, a sea monster and a hound. I've written a paper. It's very short. It just says "gosh".
Strachan's resigned. Morag Strachan, Regional Director, Scotland, has taken the sleeper south and sent her wellies to a charity shop.
That's all four Directors gone: Pryce, Ashcombe, Kerrigan and now her. Which leaves Lord Vane, and nobody to hold his coat.
There's one more Stone. The tenth. It's in the east of England, and the hum from there is a low, strange one, like a bell under a lake.
York. The Spirit Stone. And then the Moot.
Here's the good news: the road south out of Aberdeen is open. It runs down the coast to Northumberland, along Hadrian's Wall to Newcastle, over the Moors to Whitby, and on to York.
I've looked at a map. It is, in places, very straight.
And two rumours. Something is stirring on a hill in County Durham, and something large and black has been seen on the clifftop at Whitby.
The reports say 'worm' and 'dog'. I'm choosing to believe those are two separate reports.

Vane said he'd see you at the Moot. He's right. All the Keepers will be there, and the Four Winds, and a Champion nobody has beaten in twenty years. At Stonehenge. In October. I'm told it's a drizzle.
The road south is long, and the ferry from Aberdeen to Orkney sails whenever you like. The Moot can wait a morning.

aberdeen_night_baker.text: Butteries won't bake themselves. I start at midnight so the whole city has its rowies warm by breakfast.
A buttery's like a croissant that's been through an Aberdeen winter. Flatter, saltier and far tougher.
The streets are lovely and quiet at this hour. Just me, the ovens and a fox who thinks he's my apprentice.

aberdeen_astronomer.text: On a clear night you can catch the northern lights over the beach. The haar usually has other ideas.
That bright one's Jupiter. Wave if you like. It's a long way off, so it might take a while to wave back.
Granite city by day, star city by night. Well, when the clouds behave. Which is about twice a year.

then.text: Rain again. I've three essays due and an umbrella that gave up in Union Street. Bit of a theme, this term.

else.text: I'm meant to be at the library. I'm in the square instead, which is a very Aberdeen sort of study break.
A seagull stole my sandwich this morning. Fair play to it, honestly. Best thing that's happened all week.

abdn_docker.text: Forty years round this harbour and I still watch every boat come in. Pays the bills, and the view comes free.

then.text: Foghorn's been going since five. You stop hearing it. Then it stops and you can't sleep.

else.text: Supply boats, trawlers, the Orkney ferry. If it floats, it ends up on my quay sooner or later.

abdn_shopper.text: Union Street is a mile of shops and I'm only after one pair of socks. We'll see how that goes.

then.text: Granite and sunshine. It's like walking through a jewellery box. Don't tell anyone I said that.

else.text: Bus is late, tea is cold, and the city's still lovely. I can't explain it either.

abdn_jogger.text: Harbour loop, then back via the beach. Don't stop me or I'll lose my rhythm and my dignity.
Lovely town for a run, bar the hills. And the wind. And the seagulls.
